extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing poetry and for judging/criticising poetry: principles of taste, technical advice on style and sound, and moral/ethical rules for critics. Drawn from Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism (1709).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your own reach
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be sure yourself and your own reach to know / How far your genius taste and learning go. Launch not beyond your depth, but be discreet / And mark that point where sense and dullness meet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't attempt subjects or forms beyond your competence; be self-aware about limits of genius, taste and learning. Anti-pattern: overreaching ambition that produces nonsense or shallow imitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: First follow nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “First follow nature and your judgment frame / By her just standard, which is still the same.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nature (life, force, and beauty) as the primary standard; art should supply or reveal nature rather than contradict it. Works should feel organic: sound must echo sense. Example guidance: align meter/tone with content (soft lines for gentle subjects, rough for violent ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from the ancients and their context
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be Homer's works your study and delight... Know well each ancient's proper character, His fable subject scope in every page, Religion, country, genius of his age.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study classical models (esp. Homer, Horace, Longinus, Quintilian) and understand historical/cultural context before applying their precepts. Anti-pattern: copying ancient words or rules without attending to their original purpose and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are methodized nature; use them, don't worship them
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those rules, of old discovered, not devised, / Are nature still, but nature methodiz'd.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal rules as codified observations of nature; they are aids, not tyrants. Apply rules thoughtfully, not mechanically. Example: recognize when deviation (license) serves nature's end.

rubrics_metrics.name: License may be allowed but sparingly and with precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: “Great wits sometimes may gloriously offend... If, where the rules not far enough extend... Some lucky license answer to the full / The intent proposed that license is a rule... Moderns beware! or if you must offend / Against the precept, ne'er transgress its end, / Let it be seldom, and compelled by need, / And have, at least, their precedent to plead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional deviations from rules can be successful but should be rare, purposeful, and defensible by precedent or demonstrable effect. Anti-pattern: flouting rules for novelty's sake without achieving higher artistic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sound to sense (musical appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Tis not enough no harshness gives offense, / The sound must seem an echo to the sense... Soft is the strain when Zephyr gently blows... But when loud surges lash the sounding shore, / The hoarse, rough verse should like the torrent roar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary rhythm, diction, and sonic texture to reflect the poem’s emotional and narrative content. Use varying metrical motion to mirror action or passion (e.g., slow, heavy lines for effort; swift lines for speed). Anti-pattern: monotonous metre that contradicts subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit is nature dressed to advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: “True wit is nature to advantage dress'd; / What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit and originality should feel natural and reveal truth elegantly rather than by mere cleverness. Avoid ornament that hides poverty of thought—prefer modest plainness that enhances wit. Anti-pattern: ostentatious 'glittering thoughts' with no fit or coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive ornament and false eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Others for language all their care express, / And value books, as women men, for dress... Words are like leaves, and where they most abound / Much fruit of sense beneath is rarely found.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sense over style. Decorative language should not obscure meaning. Anti-patterns include flowery diction that masks weak ideas and forced archaizing or fashionable verbal tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overvaluing a single part (don't make the whole depend on a part)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Most critics, fond of some subservient art, / Still make the whole depend upon a part.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a work by its overall effect and intent, not by a single technical aspect (e.g., meter, rhyme, or a favorite principle). Avoid narrow critical obsessions that distort evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: A perfect judge reads in the author's spirit and surveys the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “A perfect judge will read each work of wit / With the same spirit that its author writ; / Survey the whole nor seek slight faults to find.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathic critical reading—understand the author's aims and the totality of the work before condemning minor faults. Avoid hypercritical picking of trivial errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regard the writer's intended ends
rubrics_metrics.description: “In every work regard the writer's end, / Since none can compass more than they intend; / And if the means be just, the conduct true, / Applause, in spite of trivial faults, is due.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality by whether the work achieves its intentions; minor deviations are forgivable if the overall effect succeeds. Anti-pattern: penalizing a poem for not being something its author never intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés, predictability, and mechanical poetic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: (examples) “Where'er you find 'the cooling western breeze,' / In the next line it 'whispers through the trees'... Then, at the last and only couplet fraught / With some unmeaning thing they call a thought, / A needless Alexandrine ends the song.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware stock phrases, predictable imagery, forced couplets, and unnecessary alexandrines. Strive for freshness in expression and economy in endings. Anti-pattern: repetitive, mechanical phrasing that lulls the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: True ease comes from art, not chance (practice produces facility)
rubrics_metrics.description: “True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, / As those move easiest who have learned to dance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluent, effortless-sounding writing is the product of disciplined craft and learning. Anti-pattern: apparent fluency that masks sloppy technique or lack of training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes in taste and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “Avoid extremes, and shun the fault of such, / Who still are pleased too little or too much.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be balanced; neither be scandalized by every novelty nor praise everything. Extreme reactions often signal pride or lack of discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid, fair, and humane in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: “In all you speak, let truth and candor shine... Good-nature and good sense must ever join; / To err is human, to forgive, divine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine honesty with courtesy. Criticism should instruct and correct, not humiliate. Praise generously where deserved and be moderate in reproach. Anti-pattern: malicious or envious attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak with seeming diffidence; be willing to acknowledge errors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be silent always, when you doubt your sense; / And speak, though sure, with seeming diffidence... But you, with pleasure, own your errors past, / And make each day a critique on the last.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a modest tone even when confident; welcome correction and revise opinions. Anti-pattern: stubborn, dogmatic critics who never admit mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being partisan, fashionable, or swayed by names/status
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some ne'er advance a judgment of their own, / But catch the spreading notion of the town... Some judge of authors names not works... A constant critic at the great man's board, / To fetch and carry nonsense for my lord.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works independently of public opinion, party lines, or the author's social standing. Avoid following trends or serving as a courtier of fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drink deep—avoid 'a little learning'
rubrics_metrics.description: “A little learning is a dangerous thing / Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial study leads to overconfidence and error; thorough, sustained learning insulates critics and writers from facile mistakes. Anti-pattern: the half-learned 'witling' who parades shallow knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse novelty for merit (old vs new)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Regard not then if wit be old or new, / But blame the false, and value still the true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ideas by truth and effectiveness rather than by novelty or antiquity. Both ancients and moderns can be valuable; reject or accept based on merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach gently: present truths as if reminding rather than reproving
rubrics_metrics.description: “Men must be taught as if you taught them not, / And things unknown proposed as things forgot.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame criticism as instruction disguised as gentle suggestion—so that readers/poets receive it without offense. Anti-pattern: blunt truths that alienate more than instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous with sound counsel; don't hoard advice
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be niggards of advice on no pretense; / For the worst avarice is that of sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share helpful criticism freely; do not withhold constructive guidance. Anti-pattern: critics who refuse to help or who use authority to silence learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain censure for the merely dull or harmlessly vain
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Tis best sometimes your censure to restrain, / And charitably let the dull be vain / Your silence there is better than your spite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes silence is more charitable than prolonged mockery; allow lesser works to exist without continual attack. Anti-pattern: relentless satirizing that keeps fools in the spotlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obscenity and licentiousness; condemn vice even if artful
rubrics_metrics.description: “No pardon vile obscenity should find, / Though wit and art conspire to move your mind; / But dullness with obscenity must prove / As shameful sure as impotence in love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excuse obscenity or corrupting content because it is cleverly written. Both moral and aesthetic considerations matter. Anti-pattern: praising artful but corrupt content without reproach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate broad learning and human knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “A knowledge both of books and human kind; / Generous converse, a soul exempt from pride.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good critics need both literary erudition and understanding of human nature; social graces and humility enhance judgment. Anti-pattern: the 'bookful blockhead' who piles learning without wisdom.
